To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the A protein of phage Mu is a three-domain protein, that the C-terminal domain of A is required for its interaction with B protein, and that the central domain of A is involved in the strand transfer step.
the A protein has three distinct functional domains and that the B protein has a domain that interacts with A protein.
two mutations of phage Mu transposase that have distinct effects on transposition lie in distinct domains of the protein.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural basis of the strand transfer reaction of transposase A protein and the interactions of A and B proteins with each other and with DNA.
a detailed analysis of the interactions of A protein with its DNA substrate, with B protein and with the DNA-B complex.
the structural organization of Mu A protein, and with the interactions of A with B proteins and with DNA.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the A protein is a modular protein in which the three domains are structurally and functionally autonomous.
the domain II mutation in the A protein affects the strand transfer reaction in vivo and the domain III mutation inactivates the A protein in its interaction with B protein in vitro.
the domain II mutation in A protein affects strand transfer, and the domain III mutation in A protein impairs its interaction with the B protein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the central domain of A protein is essential for transposition and is required for the strand transfer reaction; the C-terminal domain of A protein may be involved in interaction with B protein.
the A and B proteins of phage Mu interact with each other and with DNA in a highly coordinated manner.
the two mutations affect different aspects of transposition, namely, the strand transfer and the interaction with B protein.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the A protein has a modular structure, with the central domain (II) being responsible for strand transfer and the C-terminal domain (III) being required for interaction with B protein.

the A protein has at least two distinct functions in Mu transposition, and that the two domains of A that are involved in the two functions are located on different polypeptide subunits of the A protein dimer.
the two mutations, which have distinct effects on the transposition reaction in vivo, are located in distinct polypeptides domains.
